summary: Provides a mechanism for a host that uses 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery to get reachability services across a network that uses RPL for routing, without itself taking part in RPL. It updates RFC 6550, RFC 6775, and RFC 8505.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9010 lets a low-power IPv6 host use a network that routes with RPL, even when the host cannot run RPL. The host registers its address with a nearby router, which arranges for the rest of the network to reach it.

subtitle: Let a low-power host use RPL routing without running RPL itself.

tldr.problem: A very constrained IPv6 host may not be able to run RPL, yet still needs other nodes in the RPL network to reach its address.
tldr.mechanism: The host registers its address with a nearby 6LoWPAN router. That router advertises a route into RPL and the root coordinates registration state with the border router.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9010 updates RFC 6550, RFC 6775, and RFC 8505. RFCs 9685 and 9926 later update it.

today: RFC 9010 is a Proposed Standard and updates RFCs 6550, 6775, and 8505. It is later updated by RFC 9685 and RFC 9926.

sections.title: Why RPL Leaves Need Router Help
sections.content:
Low-power and lossy networks limit device energy, memory, and processing. RPL provides routing in these networks, but some attached hosts cannot or should not participate in RPL.

RFC 9010 calls such a host an RPL-Unaware Leaf (RUL). It uses 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery to ask its attached RPL router to advertise a route for its IPv6 address.
sections.plainLanguage: A RUL is an IPv6 host that does not run RPL. It asks a nearby RPL router to tell the network how to reach it.

sections.title: The Leaf, Router, Root, and Border Router
sections.content:
The RUL acts as a 6LoWPAN Node (6LN), and its attached RPL router acts as a 6LoWPAN Router (6LR). The 6LR advertises the host route into RPL on the leaf's behalf; the root and 6LoWPAN Border Router (6LBR) coordinate reachability and address ownership.

The RUL is treated as an external target in RPL. In Non-Storing mode, traffic between the root and serving 6LR uses IPv6-in-IPv6 encapsulation; intermediate routers can forward it without maintaining extra route state for the leaf.
sections.plainLanguage: The nearby router speaks both 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery and RPL. It advertises the leaf's address, while the root helps keep the route and address registration current.

sections.title: Registering an Address for Routing
sections.content:
A RUL uses the Extended Address Registration Option (EARO) and sets its R flag to request reachability service. It also sets the T flag so its Transaction ID can be used as the RPL path sequence. The router acknowledges whether route installation succeeded by returning the R flag in its Neighbor Advertisement.

The RPL Target option carries the address and Registration Ownership Verifier (ROVR). When the root advertises support for proxying EDAR/EDAC, the router refreshes the RPL route and the root refreshes the border-router registration. The root does not proxy the first duplicate-address check.
sections.plainLanguage: The host sets a flag when it wants routing help. The router reports whether the route was installed, and later registrations keep the route alive.

sections.title: How Registration and Traffic Flow
sections.content:
For a new address, the 6LR first checks address ownership with the 6LBR. If that succeeds, it installs a neighbor-cache entry and sends a Destination Advertisement Object (DAO) toward the RPL root. A successful DAO acknowledgement lets the router confirm routing service to the host.

For refreshes, the 6LR sends another DAO. When proxying is enabled, the root sends the corresponding registration refresh to the 6LBR. If route installation fails, or a later error invalidates the route, the router reports that routing is unavailable. Multicast listeners use MLD reports and RPL advertisements in Storing mode.
sections.plainLanguage: The first registration checks that the address is available before the router advertises it. Later messages renew the route, and the router tells the host if service stops.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Requirements
sections.content:
A RUL cannot inject RPL routing attacks because it communicates with the RPL router through 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery rather than participating in RPL. The network still needs a trust model for the routers, root, and border router; link-layer security can help protect registrations.

The RFC suggests Address-Protected Neighbor Discovery to help prove address ownership. A router retains control over which RPL instance carries the leaf's traffic, even if the leaf suggests one.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping a leaf outside RPL reduces the attacks it can make against routing. The network must still protect and trust the routers that register addresses for leaves.
